lead: A fluid element can move in four ways: it can shift, spin, stretch and shear. Vorticity measures the spin alone. The idea exists because two flows can look identical on a streamline sketch and behave very differently: one carries spin, the other does not. Pumps, turbines, aerofoils and weather models all rest on knowing which is which. Water circling a wash basin drain and water in a stirred tumbler look similar in a photograph, yet only one has vorticity. This chapter defines the spin, links it to the velocity field through the curl, and connects it to circulation.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.4 for the velocity field and its derivatives, and Chapter 2.3 for streamlines.

sections.h3: The four motions of a fluid element

blocks.text: Mark a small square of fluid with sides dx and dy, both in metres, along the x and y axes. After a short time dt, in seconds, the square has done four separate things.

items: It has moved to a new place: translation.
Its sides have grown or shrunk: linear deformation, also called linear strain.
The angle between its sides has changed from 90°: shear deformation, or shear strain.

blocks.text: Vorticity is built from the second item only. The other three are set aside.

Take the side lying along x. Its right end moves faster in the y direction than its left end by (∂v/∂x) dx, so this side turns at the rate ∂v/∂x. Take the side lying along y. Its top end moves faster in the x direction than its bottom end by (∂u/∂y) dy, so this side turns at the rate −∂u/∂y; the minus sign appears because a positive ∂u/∂y tilts it clockwise. The rotation of the element is the average of the two.

blocks.where: ω_z is the angular velocity of the element about the z axis, in rad/s, positive counterclockwise when viewed along +z; u and v are the velocity components in m/s along x and y in m.

blocks.text: Vorticity is defined as twice this angular velocity. The doubling is a convention that keeps the curl formula clean, and forgetting it is the commonest error in this chapter.

blocks.where: ζ_z is the z component of vorticity, in s⁻¹; a positive value means counterclockwise spin.

sections.h3: Vorticity as the curl, and circulation

blocks.text: In three dimensions vorticity is a vector, the curl of the velocity field.

blocks.where: ζ is the vorticity vector in s⁻¹; ∇ × is the curl operator; V is the velocity vector in m/s. Its components are ζ_x = ∂w/∂y − ∂v/∂z, ζ_y = ∂u/∂z − ∂w/∂x and ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y, with w the velocity in m/s along z.

blocks.text: Circulation Γ is the line integral of velocity around a closed curve C. It is the macroscopic version of vorticity: vorticity is the spin at a point, circulation is the total spin effect over a patch.

blocks.where: Γ is the circulation in m²/s; ds is a small step along the closed curve C in m; the integral is taken anticlockwise by the right-hand rule.

blocks.text: Stokes theorem joins the two ideas. The circulation around a loop equals the flux of vorticity through any surface stretched across that loop.

blocks.where: n is the unit normal to the surface, chosen by the right-hand rule from the direction of travel round C; dA is a small area in m².

sections.h3: Irrotational flow, and two flows that look alike

blocks.text: A flow is irrotational when ζ = 0 at every point. Elements then translate, stretch and shear, but they never spin. This does not mean the streamlines are straight. Curvature of a streamline says nothing about spin.

A free vortex is the standard irrotational swirling flow. Its velocity is v_θ = K/r, where v_θ is the tangential speed in m/s, r is the radius in m and K is a constant in m²/s. A free vortex has zero vorticity everywhere except on the axis r = 0, where the field is not defined and the vorticity is unbounded. Water draining from a wash basin comes close to this.

blocks.where: v_θ is the tangential velocity in m/s and r the radius in m. Put v_θ = K/r and you get zero; put v_θ = ωr and you get 2ω.

blocks.text: A forced vortex has v_θ = ωr, like a spinning solid disc. Its vorticity is a uniform 2ω, so it is rotational everywhere. Both vortices are compared in Chapter 2.9.

Real flow in a pipe is rotational. The speed falls from a maximum on the axis to zero at the wall, so ∂u/∂y ≠ 0 and every element off the axis is spinning. See Unit 4, Viscous Flow Through Pipes. The payoff of irrotationality is that a velocity potential exists, which is Chapter 2.7.

figure.caption: A fluid element splits its motion into four parts. Only the rotation branch feeds the vorticity, and an element whose rotation is zero is called irrotational.

spec.title: Motion of a fluid element
spec.aria: A fluid element can translate, rotate, stretch and shear, and vorticity measures only the rotation.

examples.question: A velocity field has u = 2y and v = −2x, in m/s, with x and y in metres. (a) Find the z component of vorticity. (b) Find the rate and sense of rotation of a fluid element. (c) State whether the flow is rotational. (d) Find the circulation around the square with corners (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) in metres.
steps: Write the field: u = 2y m/s, v = −2x m/s.
Differentiate v with respect to x: ∂v/∂x = −2 s⁻¹.
Differentiate u with respect to y: ∂u/∂y = 2 s⁻¹.
(b) ω_z = ζ_z / 2 = −4/2 = −2 rad/s. Negative means clockwise, so the element spins at 2 rad/s clockwise.
(c) ζ_z = −4 s⁻¹ is not zero, so the flow is rotational.
(d) Stokes theorem: Γ = ζ_z × A, with A = 1 m × 1 m = 1 m². So Γ = −4 × 1 = −4 m²/s.

Check by direct line integral of (u dx + v dy) round the square. Bottom edge y = 0, dy = 0: ∫ 2(0) dx = 0. Right edge x = 1, dx = 0: ∫ −2(1) dy from 0 to 1 = −2 m²/s. Top edge y = 1, dy = 0: ∫ 2(1) dx from 1 to 0 = −2 m²/s. Left edge x = 0, dx = 0: ∫ −2(0) dy = 0. Total = 0 − 2 − 2 + 0 = −4 m²/s, which agrees.
examples.answer: The z vorticity is −4 s⁻¹, the element spins at 2 rad/s clockwise, the circulation around the 1 m square is −4 m²/s, and the flow is rotational.
examples.check:
dv_dx = -2.0
du_dy = 2.0
zeta_z = dv_dx - du_dy
omega_z = zeta_z / 2
area = 1.0 * 1.0
gamma = zeta_z * area
print(zeta_z)
print(omega_z)
print(gamma)

traps: Reading curved streamlines as rotational flow. A free vortex curves strongly and is still irrotational, so judge by ζ = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y, never by the picture.
Dropping the factor of two. Vorticity is ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y; angular velocity is half of that. An answer of 4 rad/s where 2 rad/s is correct loses full marks.
Reversing the sign convention. ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y, not ∂u/∂y − ∂v/∂x, and positive means counterclockwise looking along +z.
Writing that a free vortex has zero vorticity everywhere. It is zero everywhere except the axis r = 0, where it is singular and unbounded.
Confusing irrotational with rigid or undeformed. An irrotational element stretches and shears freely; only its spin is zero.

quiz.q: Define vorticity and give its unit.
quiz.a: Vorticity is twice the angular velocity of a fluid element: ζ = 2ω = ∇ × V. Unit: s⁻¹, that is per second.

quiz.q: Straight parallel streamlines carry water over a flat plate, with u rising from 0 at the plate to 3 m/s at 0.1 m. Is the flow rotational near the plate? Why?
quiz.a: Rotational. Here ∂u/∂y ≈ 3/0.1 = 30 s⁻¹ and ∂v/∂x = 0, so ζ_z = 0 − 30 = −30 s⁻¹, which is not zero. Straight streamlines do not guarantee irrotational flow.

quiz.q: A field has u = 3y m/s and v = 0. Find ζ_z and the angular velocity of an element, with sense.
quiz.a: ∂v/∂x = 0 and ∂u/∂y = 3 s⁻¹. So ζ_z = 0 − 3 = −3 s⁻¹. Then ω_z = −3/2 = −1.5 rad/s, that is 1.5 rad/s clockwise.

quiz.q: A flow has uniform vorticity 10 s⁻¹ normal to a flat patch, and the closed curve around the patch encloses 0.2 m². Find the circulation around the curve.
quiz.a: By Stokes theorem Γ = ζ · A = 10 × 0.2 = 2 m²/s.

quiz.q: At radius r = 0.5 m a free vortex v_θ = K/r and a forced vortex v_θ = ωr happen to have equal tangential speed. Compare their vorticity at that radius.
quiz.a: For the free vortex ζ_z = (1/r) ∂(r v_θ)/∂r = (1/r) ∂(K)/∂r = 0, so it is irrotational away from the axis. For the forced vortex r v_θ = ωr², so ζ_z = (1/r)(2ωr) = 2ω, uniform and non-zero. Equal speed at one radius means nothing; the vorticity depends on how the speed varies with radius.

quiz.q: Does irrotational flow mean the element does not deform?
quiz.a: No. It does deform, stretching and shearing. Only its rotation is zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Weather charts plot vorticity to locate fronts and cyclones, since a pocket of strong positive vorticity marks rising air and rain. Turbomachinery designers use shed vorticity and the Kutta condition to predict the lift of a blade, which leads into Unit 5 on lift and Unit 6 on turbines. CFD codes often solve for vorticity instead of pressure, because the pressure then drops out and the vortex structures behind a blunt body become easy to see. Search next for the vorticity equation, the Helmholtz vortex theorems, the vorticity–streamfunction formulation, and particle image velocimetry (PIV) vorticity fields.
